sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: - Another front moves through the northern Panhandle into Saturday, bringing slightly increased winds and higher rain chances from Yakutat to Sumner Strait.
- Drier and cooler weather for Sunday with higher forecast confidence of fog chances for Saturday night into Sunday.
- Looking ahead, an active weather pattern picks back up on Tuesday with the next round of fronts moving across the Gulf and into the panhandle by mid week.

SHORT TERM.../through Sunday night/...A front is pushing into the panhandle Saturday morning, bringing widespread precipitation and some gusty winds to the northern inner channels. As of 4am, gusts up to 30 kt were observed near Eldred Rock and Point Couverden. These breezy conditions are expected to peak through the morning hours before gradually diminishing through the day Saturday. With the southerly surge pushing up Lynn Canal, Haines and Skagway have warmed up quite a bit. Winds at Haines continue to ebb and flow, with temperatures continuing to hover around freezing, though a more steady onshore flow is expected once the low in the northern gulf lifts inland later this morning. Until then though, the Haines Highway will likely remain cold enough for mixed precipitation or some light snow, though little to no accumulation is expected due to shadowing along the Chilkat Range.

Just a ways further north though, some minor snow accumulations of up to 2 inches are possible for the upper parts of the Klondike Highway. No significant changes to be seen to the precipitation forecast over the region, with some clearing possible by late Saturday night. This however is expected to produce a good bit of fog over the region by Sunday morning, as winds also slacken overnight before gradually building out of the north along inner channels through Sunday afternoon and evening. The timing of the increased northerly winds in the inner channels was pushed back to the later part of Sunday due to the lack of strong high pressure over the interior and the location of the low track far south of Haida Gwaii.

Monday will see a frontal band trying to push across the gulf with a weaker ridge feature across the panhandle area. Drier weather will be continuing to start left over from Sunday. As the parent low of the frontal feature is holding over the central Bering Sea the front in weakening as it gets closer winds will be diminishing, think that they will stay below Gale with the Tuesday front and not seeing significant precipitation amounts. Through the midweek and towards weekend the general pattern continues to look on active side with any potential shortwaves about the Bering Sea low being pushed into the Gulf of Alaska.

The closer to the weekend Long range solutions starting to suggest a stronger surface low moving towards the west Central Aleutians, which would push ridge to the western gulf that will shift the flow pattern around and my bring another break in the precipitation for the SE AK panhandle.

Mixed bag of aviation conditions this morning as a weak front pushes across the Gulf and into the N Panhandle with ceilings 200ft to 4500ft and visibilities as low as 1/2SM at Petersburg in intermittent Fog. For N Panhandle, MVFR flight conditions prevail with CIGS AOA 1500ft, lowest at Haines, Yakutat, and Juneau. For S panhandle terminals, LIFR to IFR continues for Petersburg and Wrangell through 18z Saturday morning, fog possibly lingering into 21z for PAPG dependent on amount of surface winds developing with arrival of the front across the north. Otherwise upper end MVFR to predominate VFR will prevail through Saturday afternoon across the S Panhandle with a big stronger high pressure lingering. However, by 09-12z, Sunday morning, anticipating a return of reduced ceilings and pockets of dense fog for the panhandle with a saturated surface and expected calm winds at the surface and aloft, likely periods of IFR to possible LIFR through Sunday morning for PAPG, PAKT, PAWG and PAJN.

Winds through this afternoon around 10 to 15 kts, strongest across the northern terminals with gusts up to 30 kts at Skagway through Saturday morning before diminishing into the evening. Winds return to near calm and variable overnight by 09z through Sunday morning. No major LLWS concerns through the TAF period.
12Z Aviation Forecast Confidence: High for wind speeds, wind directions, and precipitation Moderate to High for ceilings and visibilities Low for LIFR flight conditions Sunday morning.

Outside: Winds generally remain below 20 kts in the Gulf today, and will continue to gradually diminish behind a front that is pushing into the panhandle this morning. Weak high pressure building in the northern gulf late Saturday into Sunday will lead to further diminishing winds and also seas subsiding through the first half of Sunday. A low is expected to move south of the Panhandle Sunday into Monday, bringing a more northerly wind shift to the central and eastern gulf. The strongest northerly winds late Sunday are expected in the Southeastern Gulf of Alaska to around 20 kt. Overall more benign conditions to start the week before an active pattern resumes with a front pushing across the gulf Tuesday.

Inside: Low pressure moving into Canada this morning is leading to increased southerly winds in the northern inner channels, with Lynn Canal seeing winds gusting up to 30 kt near Point Couverden as well as around Eldred Rock as of 4am. These increased southerly winds are expected to peak through mid morning before gradually diminishing through tonight. This will likely allow for fog development across the inner channels into Sunday morning. As a low moves south of the Alaska Panhandle later in the day Sunday, northerly winds are expected to increase along N/S oriented channels. As the low passes south, the strongest northerly winds, with winds up to 25 kts, are expected in the Northern inner channels early Monday morning.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Rain and mountain snow will slowly decrease on Tuesday as an upper level trough axis swings through the forecast area, ultimately shunting the moisture toward the east.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow near the ID-NV border through early this morning. Snow levels lowering to 5500-7500 feet as precipitation ends.
- Strong gusty winds in southern areas continue from cold frontal passage, tapering off late this morning/afternoon.
- Rain showers and high mountain snow will return late Sunday through Tuesday, with snow levels 5500-7000 ft.
- Conditions trending drier Wednesday and Thursday, with near or above normal temperatures remaining through the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A potent cold front is moving southward through the area early this morning, with rain and high mountain snow continuing across far southeast Oregon, and southern Idaho. Snow levels are lowering to 5500-7500 ft along the cold front as precipitation is ending, with strong wind gusts of 30-45 mph being observed for these areas. The band of precipitation will gradually exit into Nevada/Utah/southeast Idaho by mid morning, with lingering low clouds slowly eroding from NW to SE behind it. Strong wind gusts will persist in south-central Idaho through morning and are expected to decrease by the afternoon. Elsewhere, lighter winds and dry conditions will dominate through the rest of today into Sunday as a brief ridge builds. Patchy valley fog and stratus may develop in sheltered valleys and basins overnight through Sunday morning, but cloud cover spreading into the area Sunday morning should help to limit widespread development.

The next trough will arrive Sunday afternoon/evening, spreading a warm front and precipitation into the area under southwest flow aloft. Snow levels will rise to 5500-6500 ft MSL across the north and 7000-8000 ft for the south with the initial precip onset, with several inches of accumulating wet snow expected for those higher elevations. The trough will nudge cooler air into the region on Monday, lowering snow levels down to 5500-6500 ft area-wide and bringing gusty winds to east Oregon and far southwest Idaho. The moist, southwest flow aloft will continue, maintaining shower chances throughout Monday into Tuesday. Overall, the highest precipitation totals are forecast over the west-central Idaho and Boise mountains where upslope flow will be most favored. Meanwhile, surface temperatures will remain relatively mild throughout the short term period.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Rain and mountain snow will slowly decrease on Tuesday as an upper level trough axis swings through the forecast area, ultimately shunting the moisture toward the east. Temperatures will be a few degrees cooler Tuesday night into Wednesday in the wake of the trough. A flattened upper ridge will swiftly develop over the region later Wednesday, allowing drier weather to prevail through Thursday or Friday. Models suggest a cooler, showery trough will approach the area Saturday, increasing precipitation chances and lowering temperatures by several degrees over next weekend.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Our next system will develop off the West Coast late Tuesday. An upper level low is forecast to move over southern California and towards the four corners region Wednesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Hazardous travel through this evening for the northern mountains and I-70 mountain corridor due to snow and blowing snow. Snowfall amounts greater than 12" likely in the northern tier of mountains.
- Potential for snow squalls late this morning to early afternoon with greatest threat in the mountains.
- Banded snow (initially mixed with rain) for the the plains and I-25 Corridor this afternoon. Brief heavy snow but generally light accumulations possible.
- Strong, gusty winds and areas of blowing dust across the plains this afternoon along/behind strong cold front.
- Return of mostly dry weather Sunday - Tuesday, next system may arrive by Wednesday or Thursday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: We've upgraded to a High Wind Warning for the plains along and east of I-25 this afternoon (noon-5 pm). It does appear the front is just slightly delayed, allowing for a combination of factors for stronger than earlier forecast winds. This includes;

1) Strong diurnal pressure falls in southeast Colorado, strengthening the surface gradient. 2) Very strong pressure rises in Wyoming already observed, leading to stronger isallobaric acceleration 3) Enhancement from shower development. Slight chance we see a thunderstorm on the eastern plains or mountains. 4) Growing confidence as most mesoscale models have a blast of 50 kt winds with and shortly behind the front.
While the front is initially slower, it will accelerate due to the above mentioned factors, so we still anticipate a 1-130 pm frontal passage through Denver metro.
Snow forecast totals and significant travel impacts are occurring and still on track for the high country.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Snow is ongoing across the Winter Storm Warning and Advisory areas as of late this evening. The northern Front Range zone, which includes Rocky Mountain NP, was upgraded to a Winter Storm Warning for Saturday. Looking at webcams, snow is already coming down with pretty decent rates and the best lift is yet to come. Lift will maximize in the early to mid morning to early afternoon as the upper level trough approaches and the left exit region of the jet is over the area. At the same time, a strong cold front will be moving through the area. Models continue to trend higher with QPF or the mountains, and therefore snowfall amounts. As the previous AFDs have mentioned, there is potential for snow squalls this morning and afternoon (primarily along and following the front). The best chance for snow squalls today will be in the mountains, but we can't rule one out on the plains. Even if the plains and foothills don't see a snow squall, there is still a chance for banded precipitation this afternoon and early evening. What will likely start as rain will transition to snow as temperatures drop behind the front. Areas that see heavy snow bands will experience significant decreases in visiblities and hazardous driving conditions.

High res models are showing an anticyclonic turning of the winds at the surface to around 750 to 700mb near the southern foothills. This will allow for decent upslope in the south metro, southern foothills, and Palmer Divide area. Right now, we're keeping snow accumulations below Advisory criteria with models showing a low chance (<15%) this area exceeds the 4 inch Advisory threshold. But, we still considered a Winter Weather Advisory for our southern foothills zone given the ingredients in place and the potential impacts if a heavy band does form there. For now though, we've decided to hold off on the Winter Weather Advisory in this area. For the metro, we are expecting rain to transition to snow behind the front, with the potential for some light accumulation on grasses. Road temperatures will be fairly warm, so unless a very heavy snow band develops over the area, roads should remain mostly clear on the plains. The main travel impact with any snow in the plains will be lowering visibilities.

Snow will taper off in the evening as subsidence builds in behind the departing shortwave. Temperatures will remain cooler on Sunday, with highs in the 40s to near 50 across the plains. More zonal flow will set up on Monday, with a weak disturbance moving through the flow aloft in the evening. We could see some light snow showers in the mountains as the disturbance approaches and moves through, but impacts should remain minimal.

Our next system will develop off the West Coast late Tuesday. An upper level low is forecast to move over southern California and towards the four corners region Wednesday. The exact track of this system remains relatively uncertain and it will have a big impact on the potential for precip and snow on the plains. If the track ends up trending more south, our snow chances would decrease significantly. But if the track of the upper low is closer to what the current Euro is showing, we're looking at our next chance for mountains and plains snow late Wednesday through Thursday. The current NBM has a medium chance (40%-60%) for at least a trace of snow south of I-76 with this event and around a 20% to 50% chance for at least an inch of snow for the metro and south. While there's still a lot of uncertainty with the track, these are the best probabilities for snow in the plains that I've seen so far this season.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Heading into the long term period, starting on Sunday, ridging noses in for the morning hours behind the system that impacted the forecast area on Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Heavy mountain snow will continue throughout the day Saturday, with peak gusts as high as 65 mph.
- A strong cold front will sweep through the area late Saturday morning, bringing colder temperatures and snow.
- Saturday's snowfall may be locally heavy, with reduced visibility in falling and blowing snow and minor accumulations impacting holiday travel.
- Another round of strong winds is possible (50% chance) in the wind prone areas Sunday through early Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An active day is expected across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska today with high winds, a cold front, and accumulating snow. A broad, elongated, upper-level trough will continue to move across southern Canada with the base of the trough as far south as central Oklahoma. Westerly flow aloft becomes northwesterly as the eastern branch of an upper-level ridge starts to push in on the backside of the upper-level trough ejecting eastward. 500mb flow shows a strong push of vorticity across the region between 15Z and 00Z Sunday, suggesting a strong amount of cyclonic vorticity advection associated with the incoming cold front. Vorticity continues to weaken later this evening into the overnight hours as the system continues to move off. 700mb flow is progged to be a bit more complex and active today. Stout westerly flow between 55 and 60kts continues through the early morning hours before switching northeasterly around 15Z for northern portions of the region. 700mb winds will continue to shift to the northeast throughout the day as the cold front pushes through, with all locations seeing northeasterly winds aloft by 21Z this afternoon. 700mb temperatures will drop quickly as the 700mb cold front pushes through, starting in the -4 to 0C range this morning and dropping into the -10 to -8C range by 21Z this afternoon. With a front of this strength, ample lift will be present as it pushes through the region. Luckily, the northeasterly shift of the winds will effective cut off high wind from north to south with the I-80 Summit holding onto winds for the longest time. No changes have been made to the High Wind Warnings with this forecast update. Surface temperatures will also drop quickly behind the front, with temperatures starting in the upper- 30s to mid-40s this morning and dropping to the low-20s to low-30s by 21Z this afternoon. Breezy conditions will the front will make temperatures feel closer to teens and low-20s for most locations, a big change from Friday.

Of course, with a strong cold front pushing through and temperatures dropping towards and below freezing, snow is expected this afternoon. The best snow showers are expected associated with the strong forcing with the cold front dropping through. Rain in the northern zones will switch to a rain/snow mix and then to all snow as the temperatures drop with the front. All snow is expected by 15Z this morning. All locations will see rain switching to rain/snow switching to all snow as the front pushes through throughout the day today. This transition will occur north to south, with some cooler, western zones potentially seeing snow starting early than eastern zones along and east of the Laramie Range. The mountain zones are already seeing snow as of 1am this morning. Snow will continue to fall across the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges through much of the day today, with snow starting within the next few hours for the North Laramie Range. Accumulations in the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges are expected to be between 10 and 18 inches of snow, with the highest amounts in the peaks. The North Laramie Range will see less snow, likely around 8 to 12 inches with the highest accumulations in the peaks. A Winter Weather Advisory has been issued for the North Laramie Range, while the Winter Storm Warnings for the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges remain in effect. Accumulations across the lower- elevations will be much less. With temperatures remaining much cooler across northern portions of Converse County 2 to 5 inches of snow accumulation will be possible. Locally higher amounts are possible in southern Niobrara County into northern Sioux County along the Pine Ridge. All other locations will likely see 0.5 inches to 3 inches in the highest accumulation. Breezy conditions continuing behind the front, blowing snow may be a concern as snow starts to accumulate across the region. Be on the lookout for decreasing visibility with strong winds and falling/blowing snow. Isolated locations along the Interstate corridors may see brief snow squall conditions as the initial line pushes through the region.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: No major changes. Please see previous discussion...

Heading into the long term period, starting on Sunday, ridging noses in for the morning hours behind the system that impacted the forecast area on Saturday. As we progress into the day on Sunday, by the afternoon hours, the ridge flattens with the upper level flow becoming zonal. This pattern will keep us dry, but a by product will be the increased possibility for strong winds in our known wind prones along I-25 and I-80. The 700 mb flow ramps up late Sunday with speeds approaching 50 knots and remains so through the overnight hours with the flow increasing further through Monday as speeds approach 60 knots by the late afternoon into the evening hours. With ample subsidence, negative Omega (GFS), these stronger winds have a good chance of making it down to the surface. As such, our in-house guidance indicates up to a 65% chance of high winds at Arlington/Elk Mountain, around a 40% chance along the I-80 Summit, and near 55% chance at Bordeaux for later in the day on Sunday into Monday. As we head into Tuesday, conditons look to be relatively quiet outside of a two weak shortwaves that will slide through, the first on Tuesday and another one on Wednesday. These won't bring widespread chances of precipitation but increase the threat across the mountains for the two aforementioned days. Beyond Wednesday, a transient ridge noses back in and controls weather heading into next weekend. Switching gears a bit and taking a look at temperatures, Sunday will start off chilly with lows in the upper teens to low 20s and don't expect temperatures to warm much as a cold airmass will be in place as highs only climb into the upper 30s to low 40s west of the I-25 corridor and low 40s off to the east. These cooler temperatures are short-lived, as warm air advects into the region, highs will climb back into the 40s west of I-25 and low to mid 50s east of the I-25 corridor by Monday. These "warmer" temperatures will persist through Wednesday, then look for cooler temperatures to return at the tail end of next week.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The next storm system is expected to propagate through the region from Tuesday night through Thursday. Tapping into a plume of atmospheric river moisture, this system will primarily target the southern aspects of the San Juan Mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow continues to traverse through the mountain corridors, particularly along and north of I-70, creating snow-packed roadways before tapering off late this afternoon.
- Gusty winds of 35-45+ mph and localized snow squalls are possible through early afternoon, capable of producing rapid drops in visibility.
- Brief high pressure builds in Sunday before another system enters the region by mid next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Moisture continues to stream across the region today with local traffic cameras showing snow-packed conditions along I-70 near Vail Pass and US 40 near Steamboat Springs. Snowfall will persist through the afternoon before tapering off between 5 and 6 PM. As this shortwave trough moves through, gusty winds will also become a primary concern, with gusts reaching 35 to 45 mph and locally higher speeds possible.

According to the latest high-resolution model guidance, snow squalls remain a significant threat across several mountain corridors, including I-70, primarily between 11AM and 2PM. These squalls are capable of producing intense bursts of snow, sudden wind gusts, and near-zero visibility, creating rapidly deteriorating and hazardous travel conditions. Motorists are urged to exercise extreme caution and delay travel if a Snow Squall Warnings is issued for their area.

A ridge of high pressure will begin building into the region Sunday morning, pushing any lingering precipitation chances eastward. However, isolated orographic snow showers may persist along the higher peaks of the Continental Divide. By Monday, a weak disturbance passing to our north will introduce a slight (20%) chance of snow showers across the northern mountains, though little to no accumulation is expected.

The next storm system is expected to propagate through the region from Tuesday night through Thursday. Tapping into a plume of atmospheric river moisture, this system will primarily target the southern aspects of the San Juan Mountains. Forecast models continue to fluctuate regarding potential snowfall totals, leaving considerable uncertainty in the exact amounts. Additionally, this system could reintroduce lower-elevation rain chances, currently hovering around 40-50%. Temperatures next week will run a few degrees above seasonal averages, so stay tuned to updates through the weekend as next week's forecast comes into focus.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Friday and Saturday...as the upper system departs, upper ridging will fill in behind on Friday into Saturday. Dry conditions and a slight warming trend are likely.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Quick moving upper system today, with high winds behind a cold front, snow across the mountains, and brief winter conditions on the Palmer Divide.
- Another upper storm system will likely bring precipitation to the region mid week.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Quick update to add Northern El Paso county as well as the Southern I-25 Corridor to the high wind warning, with strong gradient winds expected to effect all of the southeast Plains behind passing cold front this afternoon into the early evening.
We have also added Leadville and the lower elevations of Lake County to the winter weather advisory through the evening.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...energy moving through increasing northwest flow aloft will spread mid and high clouds across southern Colorado through daybreak. This could lead to a few snow showers by morning across the Central Mountains. Temperatures remain generally mild, with 30s and 40s across the Plains, with a few locations west of I-25 along the lee slopes in the 50s. This is where winds remain gusty, near 30 to 35 mph.

Today...lots to talk about with a quick moving upper trough digging across the Colorado. This will bring mountain snowfall, very strong winds to the Plains, hazardous conditions across the Palmer Divide, and much colder temperatures after a warm start.

Snow will increase this morning across the Central Mountains, and peak this afternoon, before dissipating this evening. Snow amounts continue to increase with each model run, and areas north of Cottonwood Pass could see 4 to 8 inches, with locally higher amounts possible. It will be windy, with gusts near 55 mph expected, producing areas of blowing snow throughout the day. A Winter Weather Advisory remain in effect through midnight tonight. For the mountains south of Cottonwood Pass, down into the La Garita Range, less than 3 inches are forecast, tapering down to none for the San Juan Range. Snow will end this evening as the upper system clears to the east.

The Palmer Divide...temperatures this morning into the noon hour will be warm, with 40s and 50s ahead of the cold front. Model guidance has slowed a bit with the frontal arrival (near 4 PM) which may be a bit late. Continued to bring the front into the Palmer Divide around noon, quickly pushing south through 2 to 3 PM. Winds will shift from westerly to northerly, and increase significantly, with gusts in excess of 50 mph through the afternoon hours. Model guidance continues to develop snow showers behind the front. QPF and snow amounts are not overly impressive, at up to 2 inches, but the winds will produce low visibility and hazardous travel. In addition, temperatures will fall quickly behind the front, down into the upper 20s to lower 30s by sunset. With precipitation falling on roadways, could there be a flash freeze potential? Much depends on precipitation type, how much falls and melts on the roadway, and if wind evaporates any sitting water. As for highlights, coordinated with NWS Boulder and both agreed that the quick hitting nature and short duration, this may be a time when shorter fused snow squall warnings and special weather statements may work out. That being said, be prepared for hazardous travel across the Palmer Divide, especially during the noon to 5 PM time frame.

The Plains...the cold front will quickly track south across the Plains this afternoon. Brisk westerly flow with turn northerly and increase by mid to late afternoon. Wind gusts near 60 mph are likely, with the highest gusts expected across the far eastern counties. There could be areas of blowing dust behind the front, and hazardous travel on east-west highways due to strong crosswinds are expected. As for precipitation, guidance is developing a narrow area of rain with the front as it pushes south across the Plains. Not expecting much overall, with mostly sprinkles ending by sunset.

Southern I-25 corridor...this area is tricky. There is some concern for downslope winds this morning along the lee slopes of the southern Sangre de Cristo range. Confidence is not overly high based on limited model x-section data, and the DESI NBM guidance has only around 30 percent probabilities. There could be a few gusts in excess of 50 mph this morning from the west, before turning northerly behind the front. We will continue to monitor observations for high winds over this area.

Tonight...winds will remain elevated as the upper trough shifts quickly east into the Central Plains. Showers tracking south with the front will bank up against the southern Sangre de Cristo Range and Raton Mesa this evening, dissipating by midnight. Little if any snow is expected above 8 kft this evening. Once precipitation ends, dry conditions will prevail into Sunday morning, and overnight lows will fall into the teens and 20s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Models in good agreement through the extended period, with an upper storm system mid week with increasing chances for precipitation.

Sunday through Tuesday...broad westerly zonal flow will prevail through the early part of the week. Temperatures will be cool on Sunday, and gusty north winds will continue near the Kansas border. Highs are forecast to reach the mid 40s across the region. Temperatures quickly warm Monday into Tuesday as westerly flow increases and enhances mixing. Winds will warm back through the 50s to lower 60s both Monday and Tuesday. Winds will remain elevated in gap wind prone areas along the I-25 corridor, with gusts 25 to 35 mph possible. Humidity values are forecast to remain above 15 percent.

Wednesday and Thursday...models in good agreement this cycle with the evolution and track of an upper storm system mid week. All guidance tracks an upper low off the southern California Coast and across the Desert Southwest. This storm track is very favorable for precipitation across southern Colorado. The main issue may be temperatures. Given the origin of the upper system, it appears on the warmer side. Mountain areas will see snowfall, especially for the San Juan and southern Sangre de Cristo ranges. For areas on the Plains, deep upslope flow wrapping around the system and an upper trowal development along the I-25 corridor by Wednesday night into Thursday morning. Again, snow progs are not overly high on the Plains given the expected QPF forecast. If colder air can coincide with the heavier precipitation, decent snowfall amounts could be possible. There is still a lot of uncertainty at this time, but model trends, AI guidance and ensembles all continue to increase QPF amounts. But it does look promising for southern Colorado to see precipitation.
Friday and Saturday...as the upper system departs, upper ridging will fill in behind on Friday into Saturday. Dry conditions and a slight warming trend are likely.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: After this system clears the area on Thursday, ensemble guidance maintains an active subtropical Pacific storm track into the western U.S., providing more opportunity for precipitation across Utah and southwest Wyoming...

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Strong downslope winds will develop across Castle Country this morning, and persist through this afternoon. Gusts in excess of 60 mph are expected, particularly from Castle Dale and Orangeville southward through Fremont Junction.
- A weak storm system will move across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming this morning bringing generally light valley rain and mountain snow.

- Dry conditions will return temporarily on Sunday before another weak system grazes northern Utah on Monday. A more potent system may impact primarily southern Utah for the latter half of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A shortwave trough associated with a deteriorating atmospheric river will track through Utah and southwest Wyoming through the overnight hours and into Saturday, bringing generally light mountain snow and valley rain with periods of moderate precipitation rates in the Bear River mountains overnight. Breezy conditions will accompany this shortwave trough, with widespread gusts of 25-35 mph arriving along, and behind, the associated cold frontal boundary, mainly across the northeastern half of the forecast area. While many locations will not see headline worthy wind gusts, the Castle Country region will see ideal conditions to support strong downsloping winds along the SR-10 corridor with peak gusts of up to 50 to 60 mph between 9AM and 2PM. Travel along SR-10 during this timeframe may become dangerous to high- profile vehicles. Current model guidance is supportive of the strongest winds materializing around 11AM to noon, with REFS 90th percentile wind gusts exceeding 65-70 mph from Emery to Fremont Junction. Wind headlines for this area will go into effect at 9AM on Saturday and are set to expire at 2PM as favorable conditions for strong winds dissipate.

Stabilizing and drying conditions will follow in the wake of this shortwave trough as a compact ridge of high pressure traverses the region on Sunday. That said, an active upstream storm track will help to send shortwave energy back into the region by Monday. A weak shortwave trough following on the heels of this brief ridge will track through the region during the day on Monday, with minimal moisture pairing with the feature. As such, another round of light, high-elevation snowfall and valley rain can be anticipated from the Ogden area northward.

Thereafter the focus then shifts toward our next large scale low pressure system moving into the region as this energy is displaced from the eastern Pacific. Ensembles remain in good agreement on this feature pivoting into the southwestern U.S. from Tuesday through Thursday, bringing potential for moderate to heavy precipitation across the southern half of the forecast area. That said, widespread precipitation across the forecast area will still be in the playing cards as this feature brings widespread moisture and lift into the region. Due to this low's modification as it tracks across the subtropical Pacific, temperatures are looking to be warm enough to favor valley rain and high elevation (7,500-8,000ft+) snowfall, so major disruptions to travel are not anticipated at this time.

After this system clears the area on Thursday, ensemble guidance maintains an active subtropical Pacific storm track into the western U.S., providing more opportunity for precipitation across Utah and southwest Wyoming... potentially looking for our first opportunity for widespread valley snowfall some time around the December 7th to 9th timeframe. Time will tell.

sections.name: Kslc
paragraphs: A cold front will cross the terminal around 14Z shifting winds to northwesterly with gusts around 25 KTS. These winds will persist through the day with speeds and gusts decreasing this afternoon. There is a 40% chance of rain showers through 16Z which may lower CIGS to near 5kft. VFR conditions will prevail through the TAF period.

REST OF UTAH AND SOUTHWEST WYOMING...A cold front crossing northern Utah and southwest Wyoming this morning will result in gusty northwesterly winds at all terminals. Showers associated with this front may lower CIGS/VIS into the IFR range at KEVW at times through this morning, otherwise VFR conditions will prevail at all terminals through the valid TAF period.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: You can trigger dangerous avalanches near and above treeline on wind-loaded slopes steeper than about 35 degrees. The most dangerous slopes face the north half of the compass. Winds will be strong enough this weekend to move snow above treeline. Give slopes a wide berth where you find recently drifted snow. You can trigger these drifts from adjacent terrain or low-angled slopes.
Seek out wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline for safer travel options.

2754.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Dylan Craaybeek
bottom_line: The avalanche danger will worsen throughout the day on Saturday with new snow and strong westerly winds. The most dangerous slopes, where you can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you, are northeast- and east-facing slopes where the wind-drifted snow is rapidly accumulating on buried weak layers. For safer travel options, seek out wind-sheltered terrain where your feet, skis, or machine easily sink deep into the snow, and you don't see any cracking in the snow as you travel across it.

2690.travel_advice: Very dangerous avalanche conditions. Travel in avalanche terrain not recommended.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: A potent storm marks a return of winter and avalanche problems to the Northern Mountains. Heavy precipitation and blowing snow increase avalanche danger throughout the day Saturday. You can trigger a large avalanche in the new snow. The most dangerous slopes are where winds blow snow into thick drifts above weak old snow on north to northeast through east slopes.

Travel in or under avalanche terrain is not recommended in the above treeline elevation band. You can find safer travel options in wind-sheltered terrain, at lower elevations, and on slopes less than about 30 degrees steep.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-3 feet of snow on the ground. Recent snow and wind are building drifts and slabs at upper elevations. You may encounter wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts. Thin snow cover and unburied obstacles, such as rocks, logs, and stumps remain a significant hazard.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: With recent snowfall and gusty winds, it's possible to encounter wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.

Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is building for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin with obstacles aplenty. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Due to minimal snow coverage at elevations below 6,000 feet, winter trailhead access is challenging. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground.
Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: Avalanche danger will increase throughout the day Saturday as strong winds drift new snow at upper elevations. You can trigger an avalanche where winds drift new snow into thicker and more connected slabs on lee slopes. The most dangerous slopes face north, northeast, and east, where new snow drifts onto a connected layer of weak old grains.
Choose wind-sheltered terrain for safer travel options.
